papers.title: Fewer Boys Were Born After Brazil's Gamma COVID-19 Wave and Pele's Death: A National Time-Series Analysis
papers.abstract: The sex ratio at birth (SRB), or secondary sex ratio, is stable, with more boys born alive, but shifts after major events. Acute stress may reduce SRB through disproportionate male fetal loss, while sexual intercourse patterns around conception are associated with offspring sex. We examined whether Brazils April 2021 Gamma-wave mortality peak was followed by an SRB decline within the previously reported stress-sensitive 3-5-month window. We analysed >81 million live births (1997-2024) from Brazils Live Birth Information System (SINASC) using pre-pandemic autoregressive forecasts with 95% prediction intervals (PIs). In July 2021, SRB was 50.951% versus 51.185% expected, below the 95% PI (50.968-51.402%), indicating fewer boys. All five macroregions were below expectation, largest in the North, including Amazonas, where Gamma was first identified. Monte Carlo simulation showed that, under usual SRB patterns, a decline with this timing and consistency across Brazil would occur about once in 200 simulations (probability 0.00467), making July 2021 unusual. In February 2023, SRB was 51.441% versus 51.220% expected, above the 95% PI (51.003-51.438%), indicating more boys, nine months after Brazil ended its COVID-19 emergency, suggesting increased sexual intercourse after pandemic relaxation. In April 2023, SRB was 50.956% versus 51.221% expected, below the 95% PI (51.004-51.439%), indicating fewer boys, four months after Peles death. A comparable UK decline followed Princess Dianas death 4-5 months later. Gamma was prespecified; later observations are hypothesis-generating. These findings highlight SRBs population-level utility and warrant investigation of stress-related and behavioural pathways; ecological design precludes causality.

papers.title: Can we Generate and Validate a Pregnancy Register for Research in the UK Greater Manchester Care Record Database Using Routine Primary Care Records
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe Greater Manchester Care Record (GMCR) integrates health and social care data for 2.8 million individuals. While it contains maternity information, identifying individual pregnancies, including timing and outcomes, is complex due to variations in healthcare interactions and recording practices. This study develops open-source code to create a pregnancy register within the GMCR using diagnosis- and procedure-based algorithm established in other databases. Methods1,448 maternity SNOMED clinical codes identified pregnancy-related primary care records among women aged 14-49 years between March 2012 and August 2023. Codes were grouped by pregnancy outcome, with a hierarchical ruling approach where multiple outcomes appeared within one episode. Pregnancy start dates were derived from hierarchical coded events or imputed using biologically plausible duration based on outcome type. Internal validation compared GMCR register episodes against Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) hospital maternity admissions; external validation compared outcome rates against published UK estimates. ResultsThe algorithm was developed across 379,832 women, identifying 880,926 pregnancies. Internal validation showed nearly half of register deliveries had a corresponding HES record, with a positive predictive value (PPV) of 48.1%and a median date difference of 17 days (IQR 1-30). External comparison revealed live birth (927.8 vs. 995.6 per 1,000 deliveries) and stillbirth (2.12 vs. 3.9 per 1,000 births) rates close to national estimates but a notable discrepancy for miscarriage (8.00 vs. 15.3 per 100 pregnancies) and termination of pregnancy (5.36 vs. 25.1 per 1,000 women). Demographic alignment was strong for maternal age (31 vs. 29.8 years) and deprivation (IMD10 median: 3 vs. 2.6), though ethnic minority representation was expectedly higher in the GMCR (37.0% vs. 28.7%). ConclusionsThis pregnancy register enriches the GMCR for maternal health research, enabling more comprehensive and regionally tailored studies to inform healthcare delivery and policy. This work represents an important first step in developing a scalable, open-source algorithmic tool to support pregnancy research across diverse populations. By making the code openly available, it can be adapted for use in federated data environments, enhancing reproducibility and collaboration.

papers.title: Knowledge, attitudes and willingness to donate gametes among university students in Ghana: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Gamete donation may widen access to assisted reproductive technology, but donor gametes remain difficult to obtain in Ghana. This institution-based cross-sectional survey assessed knowledge, attitudes and willingness to donate among 380 undergraduate students at Ho Technical University. The sample was allocated proportionately across 24 strata defined by six faculties and four academic levels; within each stratum, students who were present during scheduled classes were recruited consecutively. Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, exact tests and exploratory logistic regression. Although 88.2% of participants had heard of gamete donation and 72.4% supported it, only 42.1% said they would donate if approached. Among the 220 participants who were unwilling, 210 (95.5%) selected the response that donation felt wrong to them. Participants who perceived societal attitudes as positive had higher odds of reported willingness than those who perceived them as negative (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.08, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-7.08). Belief that donation could exhaust ones gametes was associated with lower odds of willingness (aOR 0.27, 95% CI 0.15-0.48). The conditional statement that payment would increase willingness was also associated with direct willingness (aOR 7.16, 95% CI 4.25-12.06), but the two measures overlapped conceptually. The findings identify fertility misconceptions, concerns about donation and differing views on compensation that should be considered when developing donor information, counselling and protection measures.
